fullPassage: A human being has about 10 trillion human cells, but the number of microbes living inside us is estimated to be even greater. In the early 1900s, a scientist named Elie Metchnikoff observed that certain bacteria in the digestive system seemed to be essential for human health. He proposed that maintaining a proper balance of microbes could help prevent disease and extend life. However, after Metchnikoff's death in 1916, his ideas were largely forgotten. With the discovery of antibiotics, a new era began. Antibiotics saved countless lives and seemed to possess miraculous power over infectious diseases. However, overuse of antibiotics led to unintended consequences. The war on microbes destroyed not only harmful bacteria but also beneficial ones, resulting in a rise of allergies and immune deficiencies. Scientists began to view the relationship between humans and microbes in a new light. Different microbes perform different functions that contribute to our well-being. Diverse microbes help prevent harmful germs from taking over, leaving the body unaffected by many potential threats. They also facilitate the immune system by training it to distinguish friend from foe. Without exposure to sufficient germs, the immune system may fail to develop properly. Microbes also help us digest food that would otherwise remain unprocessed. Certain vitamins that are absent from our diet are produced by gut bacteria. Some microbes even determine whether drugs become toxic in our bodies. Others regulate appetite hormones and influence the amount of body fat we store. In a remarkable experiment, scientists transplanted gut bacteria from a lean mouse into an overweight mouse, and the overweight mouse lost weight. Researchers now seek to apply this knowledge to cure diseases. By introducing or increasing beneficial germs in the body, doctors have treated patients suffering from severe diarrhea. In one case, a donor transplant of healthy gut bacteria caused the patient's symptoms to vanish entirely. Nutritionists suggest eating foods that support beneficial bacteria, such as yogurt and gimchi. They also recommend protecting existing germs by avoiding heavily processed food, as frozen food and additives can damage the microbial balance. Spending time in nature exposes us to diverse bacteria that strengthen our defenses. Above all, experts urge us to use antibiotics wisely, as overuse can damage beneficial bacteria that we need. We should think of microbes not as enemies but as part of our bodies.
title: Microbes and Health — The Hidden Heroes Inside Us
